title: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
summary: What replicated reads may return: linearizability and its real-time rule, sequential and causal consistency, why quorum overlap is not enough, eventual consistency, session guarantees and the availability tradeoff.
outcomes: Explain a consistency model as a set of allowed histories and what makes one model stronger than another
Decide whether a small history is linearizable or sequentially consistent by placing linearization points
Explain why W + R > N quorums can still return older values and how ABD write-back fixes it
Distinguish causal consistency, the four session guarantees and eventual consistency, and which stay available
Choose a consistency level for a feature, such as DynamoDB ConsistentRead or session read-your-writes

lessons.title: What a consistency model promises, and why replicas break it

blocks.md:
From the replication course you know why we keep several copies of the data: to survive crashes and to spread read load. The price is that copies are updated at different moments. A client that reads from a copy that has not caught up sees an old value, called a **stale read**.

Whether a stale read is a bug depends on what the system promised. A **consistency model** is exactly that promise: a precise statement of which results reads are allowed to return when operations run concurrently on replicated or shared data.

blocks.title: Alice tells Bob the score; Bob reads a lagging follower

scenes.caption: Simplified model: a writer sets score = 1 on the leader, which acknowledges at t = 10 ms. Replication to the follower takes 30 ms.
Alice reads from the leader at 12 to 14 ms and sees score = 1. Alice shouts the result across the room.
Bob reloads at 20 to 22 ms. The request hits the follower, which still has score = 0. Bob started after Alice finished, yet Bob sees an older state.
The follower applies the write at t = 10 + 30 = 40 ms. Any read there before 40 ms is stale. The gap is the inconsistency window.

blocks.md: This is the example Martin Kleppmann uses to explain linearizability. Bob knows their read started *after* Alice's read finished, because they heard Alice. The database cannot see that side channel, so if it wants to rule out Bob's surprise it must behave as if there were a single copy for everyone.

To talk about this precisely we need a small vocabulary, taken from the Jepsen consistency reference:

- A **process** is a logically single-threaded client. It does one operation at a time.
- An **operation** (read, write, compare-and-set) has an **invocation time** and, if it completes, a later **completion time**. Picture it as an interval.
- Two operations are **concurrent** if their intervals overlap.
- A **history** is the set of operations with their intervals and results.
- A **consistency model** is a set of histories: the ones the system is allowed to produce.

Model A is **stronger** than model B when every history A allows is also allowed by B (A is a subset of B). Stronger models rule out more surprising results, and usually cost more coordination, latency or availability.

blocks.prompt: In the figure, suppose Bob had pressed reload at 12 ms, at the same moment as Alice, and got 0 while Alice got 1. Is that a surprise a single-copy system could also produce?
blocks.reveal: No. The write was acknowledged at 10 ms, so a read invoked at 12 ms starts after the write completed and must return 1, however it overlaps Alice's read. Overlapping another read gives no freedom; only overlapping the write does. Had Bob's read run during the write, say from 4 to 6 ms, a single copy could have served Bob just before the write took effect: the order Bob, write, Alice is legal. Concurrency with the write gives freedom; once the write has completed, it is gone.

blocks.md: Consistency models judge only what clients can observe: the values returned and when calls started and ended. They say nothing about how many replicas exist or how replication works inside.

blocks.question: A system acknowledges a write, then a different client starts a read 5 seconds later and gets the old value. Which statement is correct?
options: This is always a bug in any replicated database
Whether it is allowed depends on the consistency model the system promises
It is allowed only if the two clients talk to the same replica
It cannot happen if the write was durably persisted
blocks.explain: A consistency model defines the allowed histories. Under eventual consistency this stale read is legal. Under linearizability it is forbidden, because the read started after the write completed. Durability is a separate property: DynamoDB, for example, persists a write before acknowledging it, yet its default reads may still miss it.

blocks.question: Model A allows histories {h1, h2}. Model B allows {h1, h2, h3}. Which is stronger?
options: B, because it accepts more behaviours
Neither; they are incomparable
A, because it is a subset of B
They are equivalent because both allow h1
blocks.explain: Stronger means fewer allowed histories. A is a subset of B, so every A history is also a B history and A rules out h3. Two models are incomparable only when neither set contains the other.

lessons.title: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time

blocks.md:
Herlihy and Wing defined **linearizability** in 1990. Informally: every operation appears to take effect atomically at a single instant, its **linearization point**, somewhere between its invocation and its completion. The results must match those of a single sequential copy executing the operations in the order of those points.

Two consequences follow. Operations that overlap may be ordered either way. But if operation A completes before operation B is invoked, A must come before B.

blocks.caption: S is the sequential order. Real-time precedence between non-overlapping operations must be preserved, and S must obey the object's sequential rules (a read returns the latest write in S).

blocks.md: Jepsen restates this with three constraints from Viotti and Vukolic: **SingleOrder** (one total order of all operations), **RealTime** (consistent with the real-time bound above) and **RVal** (return values obey the data type, for a register: a read returns the last write before it).

blocks.title: Placing linearization points on a register x (starts at 0)

scenes.caption: Three overlapping operations: P1 writes 1 during [1, 4], P2 reads 1 during [2, 5], P3 reads 0 during [3, 6]. Is there a single order that explains both results?
P3's read returned 0, so its point must come before the write's. Put it at 3.2, just after P3 starts.
The write takes effect at 3.5, still inside its interval [1, 4].
P2's read takes effect at 4.5 and returns 1. Order rB, w1, rA is legal and every point lies in its interval: the history is linearizable. A script confirms it is the only valid order of the 6.
Now P3 reads again during [7, 9] and gets 0. P2 finished reading 1 at time 5, before 7, so this read must see 1 or newer. No order works: not linearizable.

blocks.md: A read that overlaps a write may return either the old or the new value. Once any read has returned the new value and completed, every later-starting read must return it too. Linearizability forbids the value from flickering back.

For small histories you can check linearizability by brute force: try every total order, keep those that respect real-time precedence and the register's rules. Real checkers prune this search heavily, because the number of orders grows factorially, but the definition is exactly this loop.

blocks.title: A brute-force linearizability check

scenes.caption: The history from the figure: three overlapping operations. No operation ends before another starts, so real time constrains nothing here.
First order tried: w1, rA, rB. Real time is fine, so legal() replays it on a register starting at 0.
w1 sets x to 1. rA expects 1 and matches. rB expects 0 but x is 1, so legal() returns False.
Order rB, w1, rA: rB reads 0 from the initial state, w1 sets 1, rA reads 1. Both checks pass and the order is printed.

All 6 orders tried: only one is valid, matching the figure. Adding rC = 0 at [7, 9] would make real_time_ok reject every order where rC comes before rA or w1, and legal() rejects the rest, since rC would then have to read 1.

blocks.md:
Herlihy and Wing proved two properties that make linearizability practical:

- **Locality**: a history is linearizable if and only if the operations on each individual object are linearizable. You can build and verify each object (each key, each queue) separately.
- **Nonblocking**: a pending call of a total operation never has to wait for another pending call to finish just to stay correct.

Jepsen notes that what counts as one object varies: some stores make single keys linearizable, others whole tables. For multi-object transactions with the same real-time guarantee, the term is **strict serializability**.

Linearizability is not serializability. Serializability is about transactions over many objects appearing in *some* serial order, with no real-time rule. Linearizability is about single operations on one object, *with* the real-time rule. Their combination is strict serializability.

blocks.question: P1 writes x = 5 during [0, 10]. P2 reads x during [2, 3] and gets 5. P3 reads x during [4, 6] and gets the old value 0. Is this linearizable?
options: Yes, because all three operations overlap the write
No, because P2 completed reading 5 before P3 started, so P3 must see 5 or newer
Yes, because P3's read finished before the write finished
No, because P2 read 5 before the write had completed
blocks.explain: P2's read ([2, 3]) completes before P3's read ([4, 6]) begins, so P2 precedes P3 in any valid order. P2 returned 5, so the write precedes P2, hence P3 too, and P3 must return 5. Reading a value before its write completes (P2) is fine: the write's point can be anywhere in [0, 10].

blocks.question: Your service keeps each key linearizable on its own, using a separate replica group per key. A teammate worries that a history mixing single-key operations on many keys is therefore not linearizable as a whole. What does locality say?
options: Per-key linearizability implies the whole history of single-key operations is linearizable
The teammate is right; you need a global lock across groups
Locality only holds for sequential consistency
It depends on clock synchronization between groups
blocks.explain: Herlihy and Wing's Theorem 1: a history is linearizable iff each object's sub-history is. This covers single-key operations. An atomic operation that touches two keys at once is a different object (or a transaction), which locality does not cover.

lessons.title: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency

blocks.md: Linearizability ties the order of operations to the real-time clock. What if we drop that tie but keep a single order? Lamport defined **sequential consistency** in 1979 for multiprocessors: the result of any execution is the same as if all operations ran in *some* sequential order, and each processor's operations appear in that order in the order its program issued them.

So a sequentially consistent system may let a process lag far behind others, reading arbitrarily stale state. But all processes agree on one order, and once a process has seen some operation from another process, it never again sees a state before it.

blocks.prompt: P1 writes x = 1 during [1, 2]. Later, P2 reads x during [3, 4] and gets 0. Is the history linearizable? Is it sequentially consistent?
blocks.reveal: Not linearizable: the write completed before the read started, so the read must return 1. But it **is** sequentially consistent: the order r(x) = 0, then w(x,1) keeps each process's own program order (each did one operation) and obeys register rules. Our checker finds exactly that one order. Sequential consistency simply let P2 be behind.

blocks.md: A useful edge case: in lesson 2, P3 read 0 again during [7, 9] after P2 had read 1. That history fails linearizability, yet the order rB, rC, w1, rA is sequentially consistent: P3 is just slow. If instead **P2** itself read 0 after reading 1, it would fail sequential consistency too, because P2's own reads would go backwards.

blocks.title: Sequential consistency is not local: two registers

scenes.caption: Each process writes one register, then reads the other, and both reads return the initial 0. Registers x and y start at 0.
Look at x alone: order P2 reads 0, then P1 writes 1. Legal and keeps program order. So the x sub-history is sequentially consistent.
y alone works the same way: P1 reads 0, then P2 writes 1. Each object on its own is sequentially consistent.
Combined: r(x)=0 must precede w(x,1), which precedes r(y)=0 in P1, which precedes w(y,1), which precedes r(x)=0 in P2. A cycle, so no single order exists. Checking all 24 orders confirms it.

blocks.md: Herlihy and Wing showed sequential consistency is **not local**: every object can be sequentially consistent while the system as a whole is not. Linearizability is local, which is one reason it composes better.

**Causal consistency** relaxes further. It is built on Lamport's **happens-before** relation: operation a potentially caused b if a came earlier in the same process, or if b's process could have seen a's effect (for example by reading a value a wrote). Causal consistency requires that causally related operations appear in the same order everywhere. **Concurrent** operations, with no causal path between them, may be seen in different orders by different processes.

blocks.title: The lunch chat: what each participant may see

scenes.caption: Attiya asks 'lunch?'. Barbarella and Cyrus each read it, then reply 'yes' and 'no' independently. Both replies causally follow the question, but not each other.
Allowed under causal consistency: participants see the two concurrent replies in different orders. Nobody sees a reply before the question.
Forbidden: Cyrus's replica shows 'yes' before 'lunch?'. That breaks happens-before, since Barbarella wrote 'yes' after reading the question.
A convergent causal system adds: once all replicas have the same operations, they agree on one order. Here everyone settles on lunch?, yes, no.

blocks.md: Why accept a weaker model? Availability. Jepsen's map, based on Bailis et al., marks sequential consistency and everything stronger as unable to stay **totally available** (every non-failing node answers) on an asynchronous network during a partition. Causal consistency is **sticky available**: every client keeps making progress as long as it keeps talking to the same server. Mahajan, Alvisi and Dahlin showed that a slight strengthening, real-time causal, is the strongest model achievable in an always-available, one-way convergent system.

blocks.question: Two users concurrently edit a shared document's title and description; neither saw the other's change. Under causal consistency, what is guaranteed about the order other readers see these edits in?
options: Readers may see them in different orders, since they are concurrent
Every reader sees them in the same order
The edit that was invoked first in real time is seen first
Each reader sees them in the order they reached the leader
blocks.explain: No causal path links the two edits, so causal consistency lets replicas apply them in either order. A single agreed order is what sequential consistency adds; real-time ordering is what linearizability adds. Convergent variants only require agreement eventually.

blocks.question: Which pair of guarantees can both be offered while staying sticky available during a network partition?
options: Linearizability and sequential consistency
Sequential consistency and causal consistency
Causal consistency and read your writes
Linearizability and read your writes
blocks.explain: Per Jepsen and Bailis et al., causal consistency, PRAM and read your writes are sticky available. Sequential consistency and linearizability cannot be totally or sticky available: during a partition some nodes must refuse or block.

lessons.title: Why quorum overlap alone is not linearizable, and the fix

blocks.md: In Dynamo-style replication, N replicas hold each key, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read asks R replicas and keeps the value with the newest timestamp. Vogels' rule from *Eventually Consistent*: if W + R > N, every read set overlaps every write set. It is tempting to conclude that overlapping quorums give linearizability. They do not, and the gap is instructive.

First, what overlap buys. Simplified model: a completed write sits on exactly W of N replicas and a read picks R replicas uniformly at random. The chance that the read misses every replica holding the write is the number of R-subsets drawn from the N minus W stale replicas over all R-subsets.

blocks.caption: Zero whenever R > N minus W, which is exactly W + R > N.

blocks.title: Chance a read misses a completed write (simplified model)

scenes.caption: Computed from the formula. N=3, W=1, R=1 misses 2 times in 3. Raising R or W lowers the miss rate.
Configurations with W + R > N (3,2,2 and 5,3,3) never miss a completed write. That is the overlap guarantee, and it is all quorums give on their own.

blocks.prompt: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2. A write of v1 is in flight: replica A has it, B and C do not yet. Reader R2 asks A and B and returns v1. After R2 finishes, reader R3 asks B and C. What can R3 return?
blocks.reveal: R3 gets v0 from both B and C and returns **v0**. W + R > N held, but the write had not *completed* (it was on only one replica), so overlap promised nothing. R2's read finished before R3's started, and R2 saw v1, so linearizability required R3 to see v1 too. Kleppmann's Cambridge lecture notes use exactly this example.

blocks.title: Quorum reads that go backwards (N=3, W=2, R=2)

scenes.caption: The writer sends set(x, v1) with timestamp t1 to all three. The copy to A arrives quickly; the copies to B and C are delayed in the network.
R2 reads from the quorum {A, B}. A answers (t1, v1), B answers (t0, v0). R2 keeps the newer timestamp and returns v1.
After R2 has finished, R3 reads from the quorum {B, C}. Both still hold v0, so R3 returns v0: a newer value was seen, then an older one. Not linearizable.

blocks.md: The fix is the **ABD algorithm** (Attiya, Bar-Noy and Dolev, 1995), as presented in Kleppmann's notes. Writes are unchanged. A read collects a quorum of replies, and if they disagree it **writes back** the newest value to the stale replicas, like read repair, and returns only once the newest value is stored on a quorum. Any later read's quorum then overlaps that quorum and must see the value.

blocks.title: ABD: the reader writes back before returning

scenes.caption: Same start: only A has received (t1, v1).
R2 reads {A, B} and sees disagreement. Before returning, it sends (t1, v1) to B and waits for the ack. Now A and B, a quorum, hold v1.
R3 reads {B, C}. B now answers (t1, v1), so R3 returns v1 (and writes it back to C). The read can no longer go backwards.

blocks.md: W + R > N guarantees that a read sees every *completed* write. Linearizability also needs reads to agree with each other while a write is in flight. ABD gets that by making each read finish only after its result sits on a quorum.

Limits worth knowing, from the same notes: ABD gives linearizable get and blind set (last writer wins). With several writers, each set first reads the highest timestamp from a quorum and uses one more than it, with client ids breaking ties. A linearizable **compare-and-set** is equivalent to consensus and needs total order broadcast, for example a Raft log. And every linearizable operation must hear from a quorum, so a node cut off from a majority cannot serve it.

blocks.question: A Dynamo-style store uses N=3, W=2, R=2 with last-write-wins timestamps and no read write-back. Which anomaly can still occur?
options: A read missing a write that completed long ago
Two reads in sequence, the second returning an older value than the first while a write is in flight
A read returning a value that was never written
Writes being lost because W is not equal to N
blocks.explain: With W + R > N, every completed write is seen by later quorum reads. But during a write that has reached only some replicas, one read can see it and a later read can miss it, exactly the R2 then R3 pattern. ABD's write-back closes that gap.

blocks.question: Why can't ABD alone implement a linearizable compare-and-set on a replicated register?
options: Because it uses timestamps instead of clocks
Because it requires W = N
Because ABD reads are not linearizable
Because replicas may apply concurrent CAS operations in different orders and disagree on which succeeded
blocks.explain: ABD orders blind writes by timestamp, which is enough when a write ignores the old value. A CAS's outcome depends on the value it sees, so every replica must apply CAS operations in the same order. That is total order broadcast, which is equivalent to consensus.

lessons.title: Eventual consistency, session guarantees and real systems

blocks.md:
At the weak end sits **eventual consistency**, as Werner Vogels defined it: if no new updates are made to an object, eventually all accesses return the last updated value. The time until every observer is guaranteed to see an update is the **inconsistency window**. DNS is the classic example Vogels gives.

Kleppmann points out how weak this is: if updates never stop, the premise is never true. **Strong eventual consistency** (Shapiro et al.) is more useful: every update eventually reaches every non-faulty replica, and any two replicas that have applied the same set of updates are in the same state, regardless of order. CRDTs are designed to give exactly that.

blocks.title: How long the inconsistency window lasts (simplified model)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: each follower applies a write after an exponentially distributed delay with mean m. With m = 50 ms, a read 100 ms after the ack is stale with probability $e^{-2}$ = 0.135.
Asking two independent followers and keeping the newer value is stale only if both are: 0.018 at 100 ms. More replicas per read shrinks the window.
A slow link (m = 200 ms) stretches the window. Eventual consistency promises convergence, never a bound on how long it takes.

blocks.md:
Between eventual and causal lie the four **session guarantees** introduced by Terry and colleagues for the Bayou project in 1994. A session is one client's sequence of operations:

- **Read your writes**: a read sees the session's own earlier writes.
- **Monotonic reads**: later reads never show an older state than earlier reads.
- **Writes follow reads**: a write is ordered after the writes the session had read.
- **Monotonic writes**: the session's writes are applied everywhere in the order issued.

PRAM is exactly the first two plus monotonic writes; causal consistency is all four together.

blocks.title: Read your writes with version vectors

scenes.caption: Index i counts writes first accepted by server i (S1, S2, S3). The session's writes were the 2nd write accepted at S1 and the 1st at S2, so its write vector is [2, 1, 0].
Before a read, the client checks that the server vector dominates the session vector (every entry at least as large). S1 has [3, 1, 2]: every entry is big enough, so S1 may serve the read.
S2 has [1, 3, 2]: it has seen only 1 write from S1, but the session needs 2. Reading there could hide the session's own write, so the client skips S2.
S3 has [2, 0, 4]: it has not yet received the session write that S2 accepted, so 0 < 1 fails. Only S1 qualifies; if S1 were unreachable the read would have to wait or fail.

blocks.md: That is Terry's practical implementation: the session manager keeps a write vector and a read vector, and picks any server whose vector dominates the ones the requested guarantees need. If no reachable server qualifies, the guarantee cannot be met right now, which is why Bailis et al. classify read your writes as only **sticky available**: you must keep using a server that has your writes.

blocks.title: The single-object hierarchy and what survives a partition

scenes.caption: Arrows point from stronger to weaker models (adapted from the Jepsen map). Red cannot stay available under partition; purple is sticky available; green is totally available.
Linearizable implies sequential, which implies causal. Strict serializable adds multi-object transactions on top of linearizability.
Causal implies writes follow reads and PRAM; PRAM equals read your writes plus monotonic reads plus monotonic writes.
If every node must answer during a partition, Jepsen notes you keep writes follow reads, monotonic reads and monotonic writes, but lose read your writes and causal.

blocks.md:
Real systems let you pick per request:

- **DynamoDB** reads are eventually consistent by default. Setting `ConsistentRead` to true on GetItem, Query or Scan returns data reflecting all prior successful writes; it is supported on tables and local secondary indexes, not on global secondary indexes or streams, and eventually consistent reads cost half as much.
- **Spanner** by default (serializable isolation) provides external consistency for transactions, which its docs describe as stronger than linearizability; default reads are strong, observing every transaction committed before the read started.
- A relational database replicating asynchronously to a read replica gives eventual consistency on that replica, with an inconsistency window set by how often the log is shipped (Vogels). If the primary fails before shipping, the promoted backup returns old values.

CAP, in Gilbert and Lynch's proof, is about a single linearizable register: during a network partition you cannot have both linearizability and a response from every non-failing node. Without a partition you can have both. Kleppmann argues that precise model names beat CP and AP labels.

blocks.question: A shopping cart service lets users add items while their phone is offline and syncs later. Which model fits, and what must you design for?
options: Strong eventual consistency; design how concurrent updates merge
Linearizability; design for leader failover
Sequential consistency; design a global order of carts
Read your writes only; no merging is needed
blocks.explain: Offline writes rule out any model that needs a quorum, so linearizable and sequential are out. With replicas accepting writes independently, concurrent edits will conflict, and convergence requires a deterministic merge (a CRDT or last-writer-wins, which can drop data).

blocks.question: A user updates their profile photo, then reloads and sees the old photo. Which is the cheapest guarantee that prevents this, and how can it be provided?
options: Linearizability, by routing all reads through a consensus leader
Monotonic writes, by ordering writes per session
Read your writes, by tracking the session's write vector and reading from a server that dominates it
Eventual consistency, by waiting for replication to finish
blocks.explain: Only the user's own write must be visible to that user, which is read your writes. Terry's session vectors, or sticking the session to a replica that took the write, provide it without coordinating every read. Linearizability also prevents it, at much higher cost.

blocks.question: Which statement about consistency models is correct?
options: Eventual consistency bounds how stale a read can be
Sequential consistency forbids reading stale data
Causal consistency lets replicas show concurrent writes in different orders
Linearizability is the same as serializability
blocks.explain: Concurrent writes have no causal path, so causal replicas may order them differently. Eventual consistency gives no time bound; sequential consistency allows a process to lag arbitrarily; serializability concerns transactions with no real-time rule.
